1gum62j:231: The design choice of running scripts via bash and returning only structured JSON hides a profound engineering philosophy: leave the "uncertainty" to the LLM, leave the "certainty" to the script. Parsing resumes and generating PDFs are deterministic tasks and should be executed with deterministic code; only tasks that require generalization, like "judge whether the Skill is relevant" or "decide what to do next," are delegated to the LLM. This division makes the Skill's token consumption predictable and controllable — the LLM's non-deterministic capabilities and the deterministic script's reliability each operate at the layer they excel at, forming an efficient hybrid execution architecture.
1hzarhf:16: Ch20 AI Philosophy, Safety, and the Future
1m3tksq:264: The core philosophy of the SKILL.md spec is "Progressive Disclosure" — a pattern already mature in UI design. The core idea is to show only the information needed for the current step, without loading irrelevant content in advance. In the AI Skill context, this pattern's value is amplified: the LLM's context window is a scarce resource, and Skill designers must decide what information enters the context and when. The three-layer architecture demonstrated in the article (frontmatter metadata ~100 tokens → main body ~1350 tokens → on-demand external files) is essentially a strict resource allocation protocol, ensuring every token is spent where it matters.

1w7e39v:271: The description field design is the soul of the entire Skill. Rather than a description, it's more like a "trigger condition checklist." The article emphasizes including both positive trigger words (resume, CV, ATS-friendly) and negative boundaries (Do NOT use for: cover letters, job searching). This positive/negative checklist design lets the LLM make routing decisions without algorithmic judgment. This is a strategy of converting complex reasoning into table lookup — table lookup is far faster than reasoning and more predictable. For enterprise Skill scenarios, this determinism matters more than "clever reasoning," because a single mis-trigger can cause erroneous behavior in production.

qg6qq:261: The Gotchas pitfall checklist is one of the most valuable design patterns in the entire article. Its essence is making "tacit knowledge" — known only to human experts — explicit. An Agent won't discover on its own that WeasyPrint silently falls back to the system default serif font, nor will it naturally know that accented characters can break ATS parsing — these are things only people who have stepped on these rakes can write. Without Gotchas, the Agent can only learn through trial and error, wasting a great deal of tokens and potentially producing non-compliant output. Expert knowledge made explicit, written once and run everywhere — that is the true value of a Skill as a knowledge encapsulation unit.
